newsitem.title: ITALY: Stock watchdog pursues Olivetti probe.
newsitem.headline: Stock watchdog pursues Olivetti probe.

text.p: Italy's stock market watchdog Consob is pressing on with its scrutiny of the accounts of troubled information technology group Olivetti, this time probing its factoring debt collection operations and sale of its stake in British subsidiary Acorn.
Daily newspaper Il Sole 24 Ore said on Thursday the stock market commission had recently sent a new set of requests for clarification from the group based in Ivrea in north west Italy.

Enzo Berlanda, chairman of Consob, told Reuters Financial Television in an interview the watchdog was still examining Olivetti's accounts for the first half of 1996, a process it began back in September.

"We have asked questions and have had some answers from the shareholder-appointed internal auditors -- even though Italian law does not require their intervention in relation to half-yearly accounts," Berlanda said.
"We are however continuing to examine the first half accounts," he added.

Olivetti, which has not made a profit since 1990, has been under investigation by the watchdog since early September when then director-general Renzo Francesconi disputed the accuracy of Olivetti's first half results and resigned.
Olivetti, which has undergone a string of changes at top manager level in the last few months, has since said it is suing Francesconi for damages but Consob has continued its inquiry.

Il Sole said the latest queries involved capital gains registered in the first half accounts and were linked to Olivetti's sale in June of a 14.7 percent stake in British computer company Acorn to U.S. securities house Lehman's, giving a capital gain of 64 billion lire.
The newspaper said payment for the stake would be made in instalments as it was linked to Lehman selling Acorn shares on the market in London.

The average price for the sale was estimated at 2.10 sterling per share and part of the package had already been sold at 2.33. But in recent sessions Acorn shares had fallen to 2.00 and so the expected capital gain was no longer applicable.
Questions on factoring concerned operations for 542 billion lire at the end of June, which fell to 321 billion in August.
Berlanda also told RFTV Consob had referred its investigation into insider dealing on Olivetti shares to the public prosecutor.

"When we see anomaly in the trading of a share, an anomaly in terms of volumes and market trend, we investigate. When we see the anomaly was not a spontaneous thing but the subject of someone's initiative, we are obliged by law to report the facts with a detailed report to the prosecutor," he said.

"We saw what the market could see, that is in a certain period and in certain days, regarding volumes and trends, the price of the Olivetti share was not following the normal market trend. We have gathered the facts and reported them to the prosecutor," he added.

Olivetti shares pitched and tossed in September as rumour and fact about the state of its finances washed through the market. Trading in the stock was suspended repeatedly at the height of the crisis due to excessive price fluctuation.
Olivetti shares plummeted to all-times lows in September and have since dropped further to 435 lire per ordinary share in October. The stock was trading at 440 lire on Thursday.
